title: Optimal Euclidean error for pure-DP statistical-query release
formal: Does there exist a universal C>0 such that, for every integers n,T,k≥1, every real ε∈(0,1], and every k functions f_j:[T]→[−1,1], there is a pure ε-differentially private mechanism M with E[‖M(x)−f(x)‖₂]/√k≤C·min{1,√(ln(2T)/(εn))} for every x∈[T]^n?
why: Would determine the fundamental worst-case accuracy of pure-private statistical-query release, independently of the number of queries.
status_note: Resolved by Aleksandar Nikolov: August 2022 preprint, SODA 2023 Theorem 1, journal version 2024. The original paper explicitly resolves Open Problem 2 and uses this card’s error norm and replacement privacy model. The 3 August 2026 Fitzsimons revision confirms the prior resolution and supplies an alternative rate. No proof-assistant build or independent proof audit was performed.
review_note: Resolved-status correction after checking the original theorem, its published versions and the later revision; not an independent proof audit.

definitions: [T]={1,…,T}; the database is an ordered list x=(x₁,…,x_n). Write f(x)_j=(1/n)Σ_i f_j(x_i). The queries and ε are fixed before accessing x. A mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions M_x on ℝ^k indexed by all databases x; it may depend on n,T,k,ε and the whole query family. Pure ε-differential privacy means M_x(E)≤exp(ε)M_y(E) for every Borel set E⊆ℝ^k and every two databases differing in at most one position by replacement. The privacy requirement includes every database, without a distributional promise. In the error bound a random output is drawn from M_x and the expectation is over this output alone. ‖z‖₂=(Σ_j z_j²)^(1/2). The answer is an existence question about probability kernels, with no computational or finite-precision requirement. C is independent of all parameters and queries. The normalization is expected Euclidean norm divided by √k, rather than a maximum-coordinate bound or the square root of expected squared error. The source’s log T target has the equivalent harmless truncation and T=1 convention written here.

upgraded_from.title: Optimal Euclidean error for pure-DP statistical-query release

context_blocks.text: This question is already resolved. Nikolov’s August 2022 preprint, published at SODA 2023 and subsequently in the Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, gives the requested pure-private normalized Euclidean guarantee. Theorem 1 explicitly identifies its conclusion as the resolution of Nikolov–Ullman Open Problem 2. The source proposal was therefore stale when imported.

A statistical query is a bounded average. For a database of categories, an indicator query asks what fraction of records belong to a selected set of categories. Several queries can ask about overlapping sets, so their answers concern the same individuals. Privacy constrains the distribution of the entire released vector under replacement of any one record. Protecting each coordinate separately with the full privacy budget would not establish the required joint guarantee.

The normalized Euclidean error is the square root of the average squared coordinate error for one output, followed by expectation over the mechanism. If the error vector is (1,0,…,0), its normalized Euclidean error is 1/√k, whereas its maximum-coordinate error is one. Thus one badly estimated query can have much less effect on the average criterion. The position of the expectation also matters: this is not the square root of the expected squared error.

The 2021 question sought a bound independent of k, the number of queries. Its shifted logarithm handles a singleton universe, and the minimum with one reflects a trivial data-independent release: outputting the zero vector has normalized error at most one. A singleton universe in fact permits exact release, because all databases have the same answer vector. These conventions do not assert a matching lower bound in every parameter regime.

Nikolov proves sample complexity O(log T/(εα²)) for normalized error α, alongside sharper alternatives for some parameters. Rearranging gives the square-root accuracy bound. His definitions use bounded real queries, replacement adjacency and the expected norm divided by √k, matching this card. The mechanism exploits a lower-dimensional representation of the feasible answer vectors and also has an efficiency guarantee beyond this card’s existence requirement.

The July 2026 version of Fitzsimons’s paper focused on the maximum-coordinate problem and retained a √log(2k) factor. Its 3 August revision adds Theorem 1.2 with the exact Euclidean rate and explicitly acknowledges Nikolov’s earlier solution. The Euclidean conclusion therefore must not be classified as still open by reading only the first version or the abstract-page summary. The newer paper’s claimed formalization was not independently built or audited here.
